title: How much water you need
summary: Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day for 2 weeks, more for heat, illness, children, pregnancy and nursing, and never ration drinking water.

blocks.p: Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) of water per person per day.

list: CDC: the gallon is for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and other uses.
FEMA, the Red Cross and USDA: for drinking, plus food preparation and hygiene. An older FEMA and Red Cross guide splits it as half a gallon for drinking and half a gallon for cooking and sanitation.

blocks.p: Of that gallon, a normally active person needs about three quarters of a gallon (2.8 L) of fluid a day, from water and other drinks (Ready.gov). FEMA’s guide says to drink at least 2 quarts (1.9 L) a day.

blocks.warn: The gallon does not cover flushing toilets, bathing or laundry. None of the agencies counts water for these. Plan that water separately, and use water that is not fit to drink for it where you can.

list: At home: at least 2 weeks. CDC: at least 3 days, and a 2-week supply if possible. The Red Cross and FEMA: a 2-week supply at home.
To take with you if you leave: 3 days (Red Cross).

blocks.p: For 4 people for 2 weeks, that is at least 56 gallons (212 L). The planner works out the total for your group and the days you set.

list: Children, nursing mothers and sick people (Ready.gov).
Everyone in hot weather: in very hot temperatures, water needs can double (Ready.gov, FEMA). The planner adds 1 gallon per person per day for very hot weather.

blocks.p: No agency gives an amount for any of these except hot weather. Store more than the minimum if anyone in the group is on this list.
Ready.gov: “Never ration drinking water unless ordered to do so by authorities. Drink the amount you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.”

list: Drink what you need today, and start looking for more water while you still have some.
Lower how much your body needs: reduce activity and stay cool (Ready.gov).
Save drinking water for drinking and cooking. Use pool or spa water for washing and cleaning, never for drinking (CDC).

blocks.p: Signs that someone is not drinking enough, and what to do, are in the Dehydration protocol.
Water is heavy. A US gallon weighs 8.33 lb, and a litre weighs 1 kg (USGS).

list: Fill jugs only as full as the person who has to move them can carry. Round jugs of 3 to 6 gallons (11 to 23 L) work best, and they should be movable in case you have to take them with you (University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension).
Keep the 3-day supply for leaving in containers that are easy to carry (Red Cross).
Store the rest where it is cool and dark.

sources.name: CDC, How to Create an Emergency Water Supply (reviewed June 27, 2025)
sources.used: At least 1 gallon per person per day for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and other uses; at least 3 days, a 2-week supply if possible; store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets or a hot climate

sources.name: Ready.gov (FEMA), Water
sources.used: 1 gallon per person per day for drinking and sanitation; a normally active person needs about three quarters of a gallon of fluid daily; children, nursing mothers, sick people and a medical emergency need more; very hot temperatures can double water needs; the rationing rule quoted; reduce activity and stay cool

sources.name: FEMA, American Red Cross and USDA, Food and Water in an Emergency
sources.used: At least 1 gallon per person per day including food preparation and hygiene; at least a two-week supply; drink at least two quarts a day, hot environments can double it; never ration water, drink what you need today

sources.name: American Red Cross, Survival Kit Supplies
sources.used: One gallon per person per day; 3-day supply for evacuation, 2-week supply for home; an easy-to-carry kit

sources.name: National Disaster Education Coalition (American Red Cross, FEMA and others), Talking About Disaster: Disaster Supplies Kit
sources.used: Half a gallon a day for drinking and half a gallon for cooking and sanitation

sources.name: CDC, How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency (reviewed June 25, 2025)
sources.used: Swimming pool and spa water can be used for personal hygiene, cleaning and related uses, but not for drinking

sources.name: USGS Water Science School, Facts About Water
sources.used: A gallon of water weighs 8.33 pounds; 1 kilogram per liter; 1 gallon is 3.7854 liters (weights in the table are worked from these)

sources.name: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension, Emergency Water Supply (SAL-00006, 2021)
sources.used: Containers should be movable; round 3 to 6 gallon jugs work best; allow for the weight of water when deciding how full to fill jugs
